claim: Drosophila larvae explore their substrate by executing sequences of crawls, pauses, and turns.
source: They explore the substrate by executing sequences of crawls, pauses, and turns (Berni, 2015; Berni et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berni, 2015; Berni et al., 2012).

claim: Larvae can efficiently explore an environment even without brain input.
source: Larvae approach (or avoid) sources of odor by triggering oriented turns during chemotaxis (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011) and can also navigate through gradients of light intensity (Kane et al., 2013; Humberg and Sprecher, 2018), temperature (Luo et al., 2010; Lahiri et al., 2011), and mechanosensory cues (Jovanic et al., 2019). Their natural habitat is decaying vegetable matter distributed in patches (Ringo, 2018), and due to food decay and intraspecific competition larvae are constantly deciding what patch to visit and how long to stay before exploring for new higher quality food patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sims et al., 2019.

claim: Larvae approach or avoid sources of odor by triggering oriented turns during chemotaxis.
source: Larvae approach (or avoid) sources of odor by triggering oriented turns during chemotaxis (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gomez-Marin et al., 2011.

claim: Larvae can navigate through gradients of light intensity.
source: can also navigate through gradients of light intensity (Kane et al., 2013; Humberg and Sprecher, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kane et al., 2013 and Humberg and Sprecher, 2018.

claim: Larvae can navigate through gradients of temperature.
source: temperature (Luo et al., 2010; Lahiri et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2010 and Lahiri et al., 2011.

claim: Larvae can navigate through mechanosensory cues.
source: mechanosensory cues (Jovanic et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jovanic et al., 2019.

claim: The natural habitat of Drosophila larvae is decaying vegetable matter distributed in patches.
source: Their natural habitat is decaying vegetable matter distributed in patches (Ringo, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ringo, 2018.

claim: Crawling behavior is very demanding energetically for Drosophila larvae.
source: This constant exploration comes at a high energetic cost since crawling behavior is very demanding (Berrigan and Lighton, 1993; Berrigan and Pepin, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berrigan and Lighton, 1993 and Berrigan and Pepin, 1995.

claim: The foraging behavior of Drosophila in both larval and adult stages is influenced by the foraging (for) gene.
source: The foraging behavior of Drosophila both in the larval and adult stages is influenced by the foraging (for) gene (Sokolowski, 2001; Sokolowski et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sokolowski, 2001 and Sokolowski et al., 1997.

claim: Larvae with the rover allele crawl significantly longer paths on a yeast paste than larvae with the sitter allele.
source: Larvae with the rover allele crawl significantly longer paths on a yeast paste than larvae with the sitter allele, and a proportion of 70% rovers and 30% sitters is observed in natural populations (Sokolowski, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sokolowski, 2001.

claim: A proportion of 70% rovers and 30% sitters is observed in natural populations.
source: and a proportion of 70% rovers and 30% sitters is observed in natural populations (Sokolowski, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sokolowski, 2001.

claim: Due to the higher dispersal of rover larvae, their pupae are usually found in the ground while those from sitter are usually found on the fruit.
source: Due to the higher dispersal of rover larvae, their pupae are usually found in the ground while those from sitter are usually found on the fruit (Sokolowski et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sokolowski et al., 1986.

claim: Larvae engage in a highly exploratory movement pattern if no food is available in homogeneous substrates.
source: Previous studies on larval foraging focused on the behavior in homogeneous substrates, where larvae engage in a highly exploratory movement pattern if no food is available (Berni et al., 2012; Godoy-Herrera et al., 1984; Sims et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berni et al., 2012; Godoy-Herrera et al., 1984; and Sims et al., 2019.

claim: Larvae are more willing to leave a patch if the protein concentration is low but tend to stay in the patch if its nutritional content is adequate.
source: Previous studies have shown that larvae are more willing to leave a patch if the protein concentration is low but tend to stay in the patch if its nutritional content is adequate (Ringo, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ringo, 2018.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Larvae paused more often in the yeast substrate.
source: Larvae also paused more often in the yeast substrate (Figure 1E and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: Most pausing larvae were completely still, except for internal movements in their gut, suggesting they were digesting.
source: Most pausing larvae were completely still, except for internal movements in their gut, suggesting they were digesting (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data presented in Video 1 and inference about digestion.

claim: The total distance traveled showed a clear dependence with food quality, with yeast generating the shorter path.
source: As a consequence, the total distance traveled showed a clear dependence with food quality, with yeast, the most nutritious food, generating the shorter path and consequently often a smaller explored area (Figure 1B, F and S1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B, F and S1A.

claim: In both rover and sitter populations, larvae with a very strong handedness were found.
source: Surprisingly, in both rover and sitter populations we found larvae with a very strong handedness, meaning that larvae have individual biases when turning in homogeneous environments that do not provide orientation cues in the form of sensory stimuli (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Larvae have individual biases when turning in homogeneous environments that do not provide orientation cues in the form of sensory stimuli.
source: Surprisingly, in both rover and sitter populations we found larvae with a very strong handedness, meaning that larvae have individual biases when turning in homogeneous environments that do not provide orientation cues in the form of sensory stimuli (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1G and inference about the lack of orientation cues.

claim: No significant differences were found between the crawled distances of rovers and sitters in the substrates tested in the first 5 minutes.
source: We did not find significant differences between the crawled distances of rovers and sitters in the substrates that we tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: When resources are distributed homogenously, the genetic foraging dimorphism could not be detected.
source: Thus, when the resources are distributed homogenously, the genetic foraging dimorphism could not be detected.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of significant differences in behavior between rovers and sitters in homogeneous substrates.

claim: Larval crawling speed and probabilities to turn and to pause are behavioral elements that are adapted according to the quality of food.
source: We found that larval crawling speed and probabilities to turn and to pause are behavioral elements that are adapted according to the quality of food.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in these parameters across different food substrates.

claim: Inside sucrose patches, the percentage of time spent inside patches was 9.2% for rovers and 9.8% for sitters in simulations.
source: Inside sucrose patches, the percentage of time spent inside patches was small for both rovers and sitters (9.2% and 9.8%, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: In simulations with yeast patches, the percentage of time spent inside patches was 22.6% for rovers and 26.9% for sitters.
source: In simulations with yeast patches, the percentage of time spent inside patches was higher for both rovers (22.6%) and sitters (26.9%).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: Simulated sitter larvae remained longer inside the yeast patches due to their lower average crawling speed in the homogeneous yeast substrate experiments.
source: In spite of non-significant differences in the crawling of rovers and sitters in the homogeneous yeast substrate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–G), in our model simulated sitter larvae remained longer inside the yeast patches due to their lower (though not significantly different average crawling speed in the homogeneous yeast substrate experiments).
evidence: The claim is inferred from model behavior based on experimental data.

claim: Inside yeast and apple juice patches, larvae crawled significantly slower than outside them.
source: Inside yeast and apple juice patches, larvae crawled significantly slower than outside them (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: In yeast patches, both rovers and sitters executed fewer turns inside than outside.
source: In yeast patches, both rovers and sitters executed fewer turns inside than outside (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: All larvae made significantly more pauses inside the food patches than outside.
source: All larvae made significantly more pauses inside the food patches than outside (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Sitter larvae crawled a shorter distance in the first 5 min of the recording in the yeast and sucrose substrates.
source: As expected from the phenotype, sitter larvae crawled a shorter distance in the first 5 min of the recording in the yeast but also the sucrose substrates (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Sitter larvae had slower crawling speeds and executed fewer turns in the patchy environments than rovers.
source: In general, sitter larvae had slower crawling speeds and executed fewer turns in the patchy environments than rovers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Sitters paused more inside patches than rovers.
source: We also noticed that sitters paused more inside patches than rovers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Outside yeast and apple juice patches, the crawling speed increased but did not return to levels similar to the agar-only condition.
source: Outside yeast and apple juice patches, the crawling speed increased but did not return to levels similar to the agar-only condition, suggesting that the behavior of larvae that exit the patch is influenced by the recent food experience or that larvae might still be sensing the food (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and speculation about the cause.

claim: Rover larvae remained on average 72.6% of the experiment inside sucrose patches.
source: Rover (sitter) larvae remained on average 72.6% (72.3%) of the experiment inside sucrose, 85.7% (90.0%) inside yeast, and 75.6% (81.3%) inside apple juice patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Sitter larvae remained on average 72.3% of the experiment inside sucrose patches.
source: Rover (sitter) larvae remained on average 72.6% (72.3%) of the experiment inside sucrose, 85.7% (90.0%) inside yeast, and 75.6% (81.3%) inside apple juice patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Rover larvae remained on average 85.7% of the experiment inside yeast patches.
source: Rover (sitter) larvae remained on average 72.6% (72.3%) of the experiment inside sucrose, 85.7% (90.0%) inside yeast, and 75.6% (81.3%) inside apple juice patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Sitter larvae remained on average 90.0% of the experiment inside yeast patches.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Rover larvae remained on average 75.6% of the experiment inside apple juice patches.
source: Rover (sitter) larvae remained on average 72.6% (72.3%) of the experiment inside sucrose, 85.7% (90.0%) inside yeast, and 75.6% (81.3%) inside apple juice patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Sitter larvae remained on average 81.3% of the experiment inside apple juice patches.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The percentage of time larvae spent inside patches in the experiments was much higher than what was predicted with simulations.
source: Those values were much higher in the experiments than what we predicted with our simulations, and suggest that larvae might employ other mechanisms in addition to slower crawling and more frequent pauses to remain inside the food.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with model predictions.

claim: Larvae might employ other mechanisms in addition to slower crawling and more frequent pauses to remain inside the food.
source: Those values were much higher in the experiments than what we predicted with our simulations, and suggest that larvae might employ other mechanisms in addition to slower crawling and more frequent pauses to remain inside the food.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental results.

claim: Inward turns occur more often than outward turns at the border of the patch for the three substrates.
source: We observed that inward turns occur more often than outward turns at the border of the patch for the three substrates (Figure 3B, inward turns are shown in black).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Larvae in the agar–agar or the agar–gel border did not show any changes in their preference to turn toward the patch center.
source: Larvae in the agar–agar or the agar–gel border did not show any changes in their preference to turn toward the patch center, confirming that the behavioral change observed in response to food is specific (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The behavioral change observed in response to food is specific.
source: Larvae in the agar–agar or the agar–gel border did not show any changes in their preference to turn toward the patch center, confirming that the behavioral change observed in response to food is specific (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from control experiments showing no effect of patch borders without food.

claim: For the three types of substrates, the bias to turn inwards was clearly manifested when the larvae experienced the patch border.
source: For the three types of substrates, the bias to turn inwards was clearly manifested when the larvae experienced the patch border (patch radius: 25 mm, distance bin: 20–30 mm) (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3J.

claim: The bias to turn inwards persisted when the larva exited the patch.
source: The bias persisted when the larva exited the patch (distance bins: 30–40, 40–50, 50–60 mm).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Anosmic larvae extensively explored the patchy substrate.
source: Anosmic larvae extensively explored the patchy substrate (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Anosmic larvae exhibited a small difference in crawling speeds when comparing their behavior inside vs. outside of food patches.
source: In general, they exhibited a small difference in crawling speeds when comparing their behavior inside vs. outside of food patches (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference in speeds inside vs. outside yeast patches was non-significant for anosmic larvae.
source: Curiously, this difference in speeds was non-significant inside vs. outside yeast patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The fraction of pauses of anosmic larvae in yeast patches was smaller than that of rovers and sitters.
source: We also found that the fraction of pauses of anosmic larvae in yeast patches was smaller than that of rovers and sitters (Figures 3G and 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3G and 4D.

claim: Yeast patches are not attractive to anosmic larvae.
source: This suggests that yeast patches are not attractive to anosmic larvae, in agreement with the lower fraction of time spent inside yeast patches relative to sucrose and apple juice patches (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lower fraction of time spent inside yeast patches by anosmic larvae.

claim: In sucrose and apple juice substrates, anosmic larvae consistently increased the fraction of inward turns near the patch border.
source: In sucrose and apple juice substrates, anosmic larvae consistently increased the fraction of inward turns near the patch border (20–30 mm; Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: In yeast patches, anosmic larvae showed no bias in turning at the patch border.
source: This was not the case in the yeast patches, where no bias was detected at the patch border.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Anosmic larvae, apart from on yeast, trigger turns toward the patch center at the food–no food interface.
source: In sum, we found that anosmic larvae, apart from on yeast, trigger turns toward the patch center at the food–no food interface, suggesting that olfaction is not the only mechanism responsible for the turning bias that increases the fraction of time larvae spend inside patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the role of olfaction.

claim: Olfaction is not the only mechanism responsible for the turning bias that increases the fraction of time larvae spend inside patches.
source: In sum, we found that anosmic larvae, apart from on yeast, trigger turns toward the patch center at the food–no food interface, suggesting that olfaction is not the only mechanism responsible for the turning bias that increases the fraction of time larvae spend inside patches.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that anosmic larvae still show turning bias in sucrose and apple juice patches.

claim: Simulated rover larvae remain on average 31.1% of the simulation inside sucrose patches with distance-dependent turning bias.
source: Indeed, larvae spent three times longer inside a patch in the new simulations compared to the model without biased orientations (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A): now rover (sitter) larvae remain on average 31.1% (28.9%) of the simulation inside sucrose patches and 63.8 (68.4%) of the simulation inside the yeast patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: Simulated sitter larvae remain on average 28.9% of the simulation inside sucrose patches with distance-dependent turning bias.
source: Indeed, larvae spent three times longer inside a patch in the new simulations compared to the model without biased orientations (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A): now rover (sitter) larvae remain on average 31.1% (28.9%) of the simulation inside sucrose patches and 63.8 (68.4%) of the simulation inside the yeast patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: Simulated rover larvae remain on average 63.8% of the simulation inside yeast patches with distance-dependent turning bias.
source: Indeed, larvae spent three times longer inside a patch in the new simulations compared to the model without biased orientations (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A): now rover (sitter) larvae remain on average 31.1% (28.9%) of the simulation inside sucrose patches and 63.8 (68.4%) of the simulation inside the yeast patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: Simulated sitter larvae remain on average 68.4% of the simulation inside yeast patches with distance-dependent turning bias.
source: Indeed, larvae spent three times longer inside a patch in the new simulations compared to the model without biased orientations (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A): now rover (sitter) larvae remain on average 31.1% (28.9%) of the simulation inside sucrose patches and 63.8 (68.4%) of the simulation inside the yeast patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: Biased orientations at the patch border are an important mechanism employed by larvae to return to a food source when they detect a change in the substrate quality.
source: Therefore, biased orientations at the patch border are an important mechanism employed by larvae to return to a food source when they detect a change in the substrate quality.
evidence: The claim is inferred from model results showing increased time inside patches with biased turning.

claim: Biased orientations can be achieved without olfactory orientation cues, since anosmic animals can also perform biased turns.
source: This can be achieved without olfactory orientation cues, since anosmic animals can also perform biased turns (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: The ratio of time that simulated larvae remain inside patches was still smaller than that measured in the experiments.
source: However, the ratio of time that simulated larvae remain inside patches was still smaller than that measured in the experiments (Figures 3H and 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Other mechanisms, such as working or short-term memory, or other sensory modalities at the vicinity of the border of the patch can contribute to increasing the time inside the food.
source: We reason that other mechanisms, such as working or short-term memory (Louis et al., 2008; Schleyer et al., 2015), or other sensory modalities at the vicinity of the border of the patch (see discussion) can contribute to increasing the time inside the food.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the discrepancy between model and experimental results, with citations to support the possibility of memory mechanisms.

claim: Both rovers and sitters spent less time inside a patch as the number of patches increases.
source: As expected, both rovers and sitters spent less time inside a patch as the number of patches increases (and thus the patches radius decreases) (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Larvae spent longer inside patches in more nutritious environments, for example yeast, irrespective of the number of available patches.
source: Larvae spent longer inside patches in more nutritious environments, for example yeast, irrespective of the number of available patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: Sitter larvae consistently spent more time inside yeast patches than rovers for each number of patches.
source: Interestingly, despite the small differences we previously quantified, our results showed that sitter larvae consistently spent more time inside yeast patches than rovers for each number of patches (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Rovers and sitters explored more patches in the less nutritious substrate (sucrose).
source: Rovers and sitters explored more patches in the less nutritious substrate (sucrose), with a slightly higher fraction of visited patches for rovers in the sucrose and yeast patches (Figure 5G; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results presented in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The model predicts a trade-off between the quality of the food and the fraction of patches visited.
source: Our model predicts a trade-off between the quality of the food and the fraction of patches visited: when exploring a substrate with low-quality (high-quality) food, the larvae are more (less) likely to leave and more (fewer) patches are visited.
evidence: The claim is inferred from model simulation results.

claim: Both rovers and sitter spent half of the time inside patches when the area of food was divided in eight compared to two patches.
source: As predicted by the model, both rovers and sitter spent half of the time inside patches when the area of food was divided in eight compared to two patches (Figures 5F and 6C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 5F and 6C, D.

claim: The larvae stayed longer on the yeast patches compared to the sucrose ones.
source: Furthermore, the larvae stayed longer on the yeast patches compared to the sucrose ones (Figure 6C, D), supporting the prediction of the model that larvae will spend less time in less nutritious patches irrespective of the number of available patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C, D.

claim: Larvae spent more time looking for new patches (outside patches) when the quality of food was lower (in sucrose) compared to higher quality (yeast).
source: However, it is clear that larvae spent more time looking for new patches (outside patches, Figure 6C, D) when the quality of food was lower (in sucrose) compared to higher quality (yeast), but they did not reach more patches in our experimental timeline.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C, D.

claim: Having left a source of poor food, the larvae were more interested in exploring in search of food of better quality.
source: It is possible that having left a source of poor food, the larvae were more interested in exploring in search of food of better quality.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that larvae explore more after leaving poor food patches.

claim: Individual preferences of turning left or right in maze tests have been shown to persist across days in adult walking flies.
source: In adult walking flies, individual preferences of turning left or right in maze tests have been shown to persist across days (Buchanan et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buchanan et al., 2015.

claim: Individual preferences of turning in adult flies have been linked to anatomical differences in the synaptic distribution of bottleneck neurons downstream of the central complex.
source: and recently have been linked to anatomical differences in the synaptic distribution of bottleneck neurons downstream of the central complex (Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019.

claim: Larval individual differences in neuronal connections could define handedness.
source: It is therefore possible that, as found in adults, larval individual differences in neuronal connections could define handedness.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from findings in adult flies.

claim: The differences in foraging behavior of rovers and sitters are not as drastic as previously reported.
source: The differences we found in the foraging behavior of rovers and sitters are not as drastic as previously reported, where the length of the path of rovers was roughly twice that of sitters when crawling in a yeast paste for 5 min (Sokolowski, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of current experimental data with previously published results.

claim: The presence of a patch border plays a significant role for the foraging polymorphism phenotypic expression.
source: It is possible that the presence of a patch border plays a significant role for the foraging polymorphism phenotypic expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that differences between rovers and sitters are more apparent in patchy environments.

claim: A set of behavioral elements – the crawling speed, frequency and biasing of turns, and fraction of pauses – adapt when larvae explore environments with a patchy distribution of food sources.
source: In summary, we have identified a set of behavioral elements – the crawling speed, frequency and biasing of turns, and fraction of pauses – that adapt when larvae explore environments with a patchy distribution of food sources.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in these parameters in patchy environments.

claim: This adaptation leads to an efficient substrate exploration, as larvae either increase the time inside nutritious food patches or continue exploring the substrate depending on the local quality of food.
source: This adaptation leads to an efficient substrate exploration, as larvae either increase the time inside nutritious food patches or continue exploring the substrate depending on the local quality of food.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations of larval behavior in different food conditions.

claim: Food quality controls the traveled distance by modulating crawling speed and frequency of pauses and turns.
source: Food quality controls the traveled distance by modulating crawling speed and frequency of pauses and turns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing these parameters change with food quality.

claim: Food distribution, and in particular the food–no food interface, controls turning behavior, stimulating turns toward the food when reaching the patch border.
source: Food distribution, and in particular the food–no food interface, controls turning behavior, stimulating turns toward the food when reaching the patch border and increasing the proportion of time spent within patches of food.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased inward turns at patch borders.

claim: The polymorphism in the foraging gene (rover–sitter) of the larvae adjusts the magnitude of the behavioral response to different food conditions.
source: Finally, the polymorphism in the foraging gene (rover–sitter) of the larvae adjusts the magnitude of the behavioral response to different food conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differences in behavior between rovers and sitters in different food conditions.

claim: The three different substrates (agar, sucrose, yeast) had the same agar density but distinct nutritional quality.
source: The three different substrates (agar, sucrose, yeast) had the same agar density but distinct nutritional quality (with yeast being the richest due to its high content of protein) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the composition of the substrates and the experimental design.

claim: Yeast is the richest substrate due to its high content of protein.
source: The three different substrates (agar, sucrose, yeast) had the same agar density but distinct nutritional quality (with yeast being the richest due to its high content of protein) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the nutritional composition of yeast.

claim: The Ramer–Douglas–Peucker algorithm was used to identify salient turning points in the trajectory.
source: To identify salient turning points in the trajectory and to obtain the distribution of turning angles of each larva, we used the Ramer–Douglas–Peucker algorithm (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: A preferential orientation – clockwise (CW) or counter-clockwise (CCW) – is present in many trajectories.
source: Interestingly, we observed that a preferential orientation – clockwise (CW) or counter-clockwise (CCW) – is present in many trajectories, and the paths described often have circular shapes (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data presented in Figure 1B.
